newsitem.title: SWEDEN: ANALYSIS - Crown in focus of Sweden inflation report.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS - Crown in focus of Sweden inflation report.

text.p: The crown will be in the spotlight instead of inflation when Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, presents its first inflation report for 1997 on Thursday, economists and analysts said on Tuesday.
"The market's focus will be what the Riksbank's attitude is towards the crown," said Peter Granqvist, economist at Swedbank.
"The market wants to know how big an effect the weakening of the crown will have on inflation, on economic growth and on the chances for the Riksbank to lower the repo rate."
The crown traded at around 4.58 to the mark on Tuesday compared with around 4.41 last December when the Riksbank presented its previous inflation report.

The Trade Currency Weighted (TCW) index, which measures the value of the crown against a basket of world currencies, has risen to 123.48 from 117.10. But there will still be strong interest in any comments on inflation.

February's Prospera survey on inflation expectations, commissioned by the Riksbank, showed inflation expectations were higher than in the previous survey. But Granqvist does not see any big problems with this.
"It was really just that we were coming from a really low level," he said.

The latest Prospera survey found expectations of annualised inflation at 1.5 percent in a year's time, 1.7 percent in two years and 2.0 percent in five years. Annual inflation expectations for one and two years had increased by about 0.10 percent from the previous survey.
Peter Lindqvist, economist at HSBC Midland, said most of this increase in expectations was temporary.
"Prospera's survey was out before the Consumer Price Index (CPI) figures for February were released and I think expectations will go down again in the next survey," he said.

Consumer prices in February surprised the market by falling 0.1 percent month-on-month and 0.4 percent year-on-year, the fifth consecutive monthly fall. A Reuters poll had found the market expecting a rise of 0.2 percent from January.

Economists seemed also to be in agreement that the Riksbank will probably not preclude further cuts to the repo rate, its key tool for controlling money market liquidity. The repo rate, currently at 4.10 percent, was last lowered on December 17 as the last inflation report was released.

Olle Djerf, head of Nordbanken's economic unit, said Thursday's report would include some formula in keeping with the line that there is limited room for easing monetary policy but saying the Riksbank must analyse incoming information.
"I would think that they don't want to close the door permanently," Djerf said.
In December's inflation report, the Riksbank said:
"The additional room that may exist for lowering the repo rate is limited...time is therefore required in which to evaluate what has happened and analyse the situation"
Riksbank will release its inflation report on Thursday, March 20 at 0900 GMT.
